# How to Explain a Hard Topic to a Child at Their Level, Not Yours

> **In short:** Describe your child's age and what they already know, then ask for one explanation, one everyday example and a question that checks understanding. The key limit: the assistant does not know your child, so you must check the facts and judge the fit yourself.

You already know how to start a chat and send a message. In this guide you'll learn a repeatable way to get explanations pitched at a child's level, not an adult's. You'll build a short "child profile," ask for an explanation in steps, test whether it landed, and save the profile for next time. This works for parents, grandparents, tutors and anyone who explains things to kids.

## Before you start
- An account with an AI chat assistant, and the ability to start a new chat and send a message. We're assuming you already have this.
- A notes app or a document where you can save text.
- About 15 to 20 minutes. A paid plan is not needed for this workflow, though some tools limit how long or how often free chats can run.
- A topic your child is curious about, such as why the sky is blue or how a battery works.

## Step 1 — Write a short profile of your child

Start a new chat. You'll see an empty conversation with a message box at the bottom. Type a short profile of your child before you ask anything about the topic. Include their age, what they already know about related subjects, and one thing they love. The assistant has no idea who your child is, so this profile is the only way it can aim for the right level. Keep it to three or four sentences. Then send it. Usually the assistant replies with a short acknowledgment and a sign it will keep your details in mind, and that reply appears below your message.

If it looks different: some tools may respond with a longer answer or ask a follow-up question. That's fine. Just answer briefly and continue. If you don't see a message box, look for a text field near the bottom of the screen.

💬 Example: "My child is [child's age] years old. They already know [what they know]. They love [a favorite thing]. Please keep this in mind for every explanation in this chat."

You'll know it worked when the assistant confirms it has your child's details and you see your message sitting above its reply.

## Step 2 — Ask for one explanation with one everyday example

Now name the hard topic and set the rules. Tell the assistant how many sentences to use, what kind of example to use, and which words it should avoid. Specific limits work better than a general request like "make it simple." After you send, the answer appears below your message, usually as a few short paragraphs. Read it the way your child would: do the words feel familiar? Is there a single idea per sentence?

If it looks different: if the answer is long or full of technical words, don't argue with it. Reply with one short sentence like "Shorter, please" and move on to Step 4.

💬 Example: "Explain [hard topic] in [number] short sentences a [child's age]-year-old can follow. Use one everyday example from [a familiar place]. Don't use any word you haven't explained."

You'll know it worked when the explanation has short sentences, one clear example from your child's world, and no unexplained jargon.

## Step 3 — Ask for a check question

An explanation can sound clear to you and still miss the child. So ask the assistant for questions your child can answer in their own words. Ask for open questions, not yes-or-no ones, because "Yes" doesn't show understanding. Tell the assistant not to reveal the answers yet, so you can use the questions as written. Read them aloud before using them, and make sure they match the vocabulary you've already used.

If it looks different: if the questions are too hard or too easy, you can ask for a different set in the same chat. The profile you saved in Step 1 keeps working, so you don't need to repeat it.

💬 Example: "Now give me two questions my [child's age]-year-old can answer in their own words to show they understand [hard topic]. Don't give the answers yet."

You'll know it worked when you have two questions that ask your child to explain or predict something, not just repeat a word back.

## Step 4 — Adjust the level, then check the facts

Here's the technique that makes this workflow reliable. After you've looked at the explanation, send a specific correction, such as "too hard" or "too babyish," and ask for a rewrite with one changed thing. Then ask a second question that many people skip: which part was simplified so much that it might be wrong? Simplifying is useful, but it can quietly drop an important detail. Ask the assistant to name the risky part, and then check that part against a book, a trusted website or your child's teacher.

If it looks different: if the assistant gives you a vague answer to the accuracy question, ask it to list one sentence it would change if it had more room. Then check that sentence yourself. The assistant cannot see the child's face or tell whether they understood. Only you can judge that.

💬 Example: "That's still too hard. Rewrite your explanation using only words a [child's age]-year-old would hear at school. Then tell me which sentence might be wrong or too simplified."

You'll know it worked when the rewrite is simpler, and the assistant points to a specific sentence you can verify.

## Step 5 — Save the profile for next time

Copy your child profile from Step 1, plus the explanation you liked best, into your notes app. Give the note a clear title, like "Child profile and explanations." Many AI assistants also let you save standing instructions, sometimes under names like Projects or custom instructions. If you see something similar in the settings or sidebar, paste your profile there. If you don't, the notes app works fine: just paste the profile at the top of any future chat.

If it looks different: the exact feature names and locations change over time, so look for anything about saving instructions, and check the tool's own help section for the current steps.

💬 Example: "Reminder for this chat: my child is [child's age] years old, already knows [what they know], and loves [a favorite thing]. Please keep this in mind for every answer."

You'll know it worked when your profile is saved somewhere you can find it, and you can paste it into a new chat in under a minute.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending the topic without the child's age.** The assistant then guesses a level, and the guess is often too advanced or too childish. Fix it by always sending your profile first, even when you're in a hurry.
- **Accepting the first answer without a check.** Simpler explanations can drop important details. Fix it by asking which sentence might be wrong (Step 4) and verifying that sentence with a reliable source.
- **Treating the assistant as if it knows your child.** It only knows what you typed. Fix it by choosing the example yourself, using something from your child's real life, like their bike, their school lunch or a pet.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** When your child asks why the moon changes shape at dinner, you can get a clear answer pitched at their age, with one example from your kitchen or backyard, and a question to check they got it.
- **For your business or work:** If you tutor, coach or train new staff, the same workflow helps you explain a complicated process at the level of the person in front of you. You still review every fact before you share it.
- **If you want to go further:** Build a small library of profiles, one for each child or student, and keep a list of the questions that worked well. Over time you'll learn which example types make each child light up.

## Try it now

Open a new chat and send your child's age and one thing they already know, in one short message. Then ask for a three-sentence explanation of a topic they asked about this week, with one everyday example. Read it aloud and ask yourself: would my child follow every word?
